question: An 80-year-old man is admitted with a sudden picture of aphasia and right hemiparesis. As background highlights, hypertension, well controlled diet and cognitive impairment in the last year under study by his neurologist. Emergency cranial CT demonstrates a left frontal lobar hematoma without contrast enhancement. What is the most likely cause of the hematoma?

options.opa: Arteriovenous malformation masked by the acute hematoma.
options.opc: Vasculitis isolated from the nervous system.

enhanced_information: The most likely cause of the hematoma in the 80-year-old man with aphasia and right hemiparesis is chronic arterial hypertension, not amyloid cerebral angiopathy. Chronic arterial hypertension can lead to weakening of blood vessel walls, increasing the risk of hemorrhage, which aligns with the presentation of a left frontal lobar hematoma without contrast enhancement on CT. The evidence paths support the relationship between hypertension and vessel fragility, reinforcing the role of chronic arterial hypertension in this case.
analysis: The most likely cause of the left frontal lobar hematoma in the 80-year-old man with chronic arterial hypertension, aphasia, and right hemiparesis is chronic arterial hypertension itself. Chronic arterial hypertension can lead to vessel wall weakening, increasing the risk of hemorrhage, which aligns with the presentation on CT. While amyloid cerebral angiopathy is a consideration in older individuals, the evidence strongly supports chronic arterial hypertension as the primary cause in this case.
